source.title: Faster Neural Network Training with Data Echoing
source.authors: Da-Mi Choi; A. Passos; Christopher J. Shallue; G. Dahl

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper through its appendices; no material cutoff or garbling affects the reported findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out predictive performance after changing the training data stream, a different intervention from the listed versions. It does not measure the training–test error gap or any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own out-of-sample performance results for data echoing. These bear on generalization broadly, but not on any of V1–V8 as specified. The paper also discusses prior work on generalization; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests data echoing's efficiency and preservation of validation performance, not any of V1–V8. Its batch-size sweeps measure fresh examples needed to reach a target, rather than held-out performance under equal epoch budgets, so they do not test V5. References to large-batch training and dropout do not constitute tests.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: every tested workload had at least one echoing variant that reduced fresh-example reads while reaching target predictive performance, and network-streamed ImageNet training achieved a 3.25-fold walltime speedup. The authors also report preserved best validation performance in the two fixed-fresh-example-budget experiments; practical speedups depend on an upstream bottleneck.
record.recipe_differences: Data echoing repeats examples or batches in the input pipeline and tunes training hyperparameters to reach an out-of-sample target; the listed claim versions concern other interventions and measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with echoing insertion point, echoing factor, batch size, and shuffle buffer size. ImageNet walltime speedup was measured with echoing before augmentation and cloud-storage input.

fits_no_version.finding: Every tested workload had an echoing variant requiring fewer fresh examples to reach its target. Batch echoing on ResNet-50 required approximately the baseline count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data echoing can reduce upstream data-processing work needed to reach target held-out performance, with benefits depending on pipeline placement, echoing factor, batch size and shuffling.

fits_no_version.finding: Example echoing before augmentation achieved a 3.25-fold walltime speedup at echoing factor 5 for ResNet-50 on network-streamed ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data echoing can accelerate training when upstream data delivery is the bottleneck.

fits_no_version.finding: At the selected fixed fresh-example budgets, all tested echoing variants matched or exceeded baseline best validation performance on LM1B and ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suitably tuned data echoing can preserve best validation performance while using more downstream computation per fresh example.

record.problems: The principal comparisons report fresh-example counts as a proxy for walltime; the walltime test is a specific ResNet-50/ImageNet cloud-streaming setup. Numeric values for most comparisons are presented in figures rather than transcribed in the text. Hyperparameters were searched, but results are limited to the tested workloads and targets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional findings on V1–V8 were reported. The paper's cited prior-work results and figure-only curve points without corresponding textual values were not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Large- versus small-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets, and adaptations that remove any penalty.
Effects of adding or removing dropout on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, not judgments that the data-echoing findings are unreadable or absent. These method-performance results belong under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test performance.
No width sweep around the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Batch size is varied, but the study does not test large-batch generalization gaps under fixed epoch budgets.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Example echoing before augmentation, with separately tuned hyperparameters for each echoing factor.
rows.baseline: No echoing; exact walltime not stated
rows.note: Five runs per echoing factor; the text says the walltime reduction is slightly lower than the reduction in fresh examples because of echoing overhead.
rows.check: The 3.25-fold walltime speedup is a method-performance result, not evidence for V1–V8. Hyperparameters were selected using time to 75.3% validation accuracy; reported walltime was measured to 75%.

rows.check: The useful echoing-factor range measures data-reuse efficiency, not a specified generalization effect.
